### **You** `00:54`

PROJECT: DeckView — an Android app to be BUILT FROM SCRATCH (no existing source code exists). Product owner: Ignacio (LyAi Labs). Package namespace: dev.lyai.deckview.*

PRODUCT: A Hearthstone deck tracker with an integrated AI CHAT interface (assistant answers in Markdown).

CONFIRMED CORE INPUT MECHANISM (decided by product owner): real-time SCREEN CAPTURE via Android MediaProjection. Hearthstone runs on the SAME Android device; DeckView observes the game screen, recognizes cards / board / deck state via computer vision or AI, tracks the deck, and an AI chat comments and answers questions in Markdown.
WHY screen-capture (not log parsing): on Android you CANNOT read another app's files (sandbox), unlike PC trackers (Hearthstone Deck Tracker, Firestone) that parse Power.log. Screen capture + vision is the only viable on-device path.

ALREADY BUILT (prototype to reuse/learn from): dev.lyai.deckview.spike — a MediaProjection screen-capture harness. Captures 800x360 at ~33-60fps, logs per-frame proc_ms/inter_ms and process CPU, and dumps JPEG frames on jank (2 FPS "dataset" mode). It is effectively the prototype of the capture pipeline.

PERFORMANCE DIAGNOSIS (established with high confidence from real capture logs — bake these lessons into the plan):
- Per-frame processing is trivial (proc_ms ~2ms median). Not compute-bound.
- The app suffered multi-second UI FREEZES: inter-frame gaps up to 3.9s, costing 26-55% of wall-clock time in sessions where a LONG Markdown AI chat message was on screen.
- Capture-process CPU DROPS during freezes and an independent ~2s timer NEVER stalled -> the freeze is a BLOCKED render/UI thread waiting on something, NOT heavy compute and NOT OS suspension.
- Freezes correlated with rendering LONG Markdown chat messages, NOT with the capture/JPEG-dump machinery (the session that dumped the most frames was the SMOOTHEST).
- CONCLUSION: the #1 stability risk is MAIN-THREAD BLOCKING while rendering long Markdown chat messages. The architecture MUST parse/measure Markdown OFF the UI thread, virtualize the chat list, and stream/paginate incrementally.

HARD PRIORITY (product owner): STABILITY FIRST — zero crashes, smooth end-to-end (LyAi "PDS Gold Rule": no crashes in production, 99.99% uptime). Accuracy and features are secondary to never freezing/crashing.

LyAi ORGANIZATION CONSTRAINTS (must respect in every recommendation):
- Any action costing >= $0.10 requires explicit authorization from Ignacio.
- STRONGLY prefer FREE APIs: Gemini 2.5-flash (free) is the default for vision + chat. Avoid paid APIs (Imagen 4, Google Places, paid cloud vision) unless flagged as needing authorization.
- Privacy/on-device is a plus; screen contents may be sensitive.
- This exercise is PLANNING ONLY. No build/deploy. "Propuesta antes de aplicar."


=== YOUR RESEARCH DIMENSION: ai-chat-integration ===
Research/design: the AI chat brain of a Hearthstone assistant. Cover: (1) how to GROUND the assistant in live game state — feed the recognized deck/board/hand + a Hearthstone card DB (HearthstoneJSON) into the prompt/context so answers are about the CURRENT game; (2) streaming responses with Markdown output; using Gemini 2.5-flash (FREE, LyAi default) as the model, with a clean abstraction to swap models (e.g. Claude) later; (3) conversation/session state, context-window management as the game evolves, and keeping the assistant honest (no hallucinated cards); (4) request/response threading so network + parsing never touch the UI thread; (5) offline/degraded behavior when no model is reachable. Use WebSearch/WebFetch to verify Gemini streaming API + free-tier limits; cite and mark confidence.

Return structured findings. Be concrete and implementable, not generic. Prioritize the STABILITY-FIRST mandate.

=== RESEARCH DIGEST (all dimensions) ===
## hs-recognition
SUMMARY: On Android, screen capture + computer vision is the only viable path to read Hearthstone game state, because the OS sandbox blocks reading another app's Power.log (what every PC tracker — HDT, Firestone, HSTracker — actually uses). From rendered frames you can realistically extract game PHASE, hero/class, mana crystals, turn, mulligan hand, the card currently being played (it animates large to center — easiest target), board minions, and hero power/secrets. The proven recognition technique for Hearthstone specifically is perceptual hashing (pHash + Hamming distance) of fixed screen ROIs against a precomputed reference DB, NOT OpenCV template matching (documented as inaccurate/slow for a growing card set). The authoritative card DB is HearthstoneJSON (cardId + numeric dbfId, plus a 256x/512x card-art render API to build the reference hashes); decks and card counts are encoded as the base64/varint deckstring keyed on dbfId, with reference tooling in HearthSim's python-hearthstone / hearthstone-deckstrings. The single biggest accuracy AND stability lever is to have the user IMPORT their own deck as a deckstring: recognition then only has to match drawn/played cards against 30 known candidates rather than the full ~4000-card open set. Critically for the STABILITY-FIRST mandate: recognition must run entirely OFF the capture/UI thread, be event-driven (triggered on scene-change/stable frames, not every frame), and the 800x360 resolution the spike harness used is too low for reliable in-hand card-ART recognition — you must recognize from large elements (played-card animation, board minions, gems, OCR'd names) and/or raise ROI resolution selectively.
KEY FINDINGS: [high] Screen capture is genuinely the only on-device option: Android's app sandbox prevents DeckView from reading Hearthstone's Power.log, which is exactly what every mainstream PC tracker relies on (log parsing + memory reading). No mainstream on-device Android screen-recognition tracker exists — this validates the approach's novelty but also means little prior art to copy. | [high] Perceptual hashing (pHash, 64-bit, Hamming-distance match) of fixed screen ROIs is the field-proven technique for Hearthstone card/hero recognition and should be the primary method — not OpenCV template matching, which is documented as inaccurate and slow for a growing card database due to scale/lighting/distortion variation. | [high] HearthstoneJSON is the authoritative card DB and also serves the reference art needed to build the pHash database. Cards have a string cardId (e.g. EX1_001) and a numeric dbfId (e.g. Leeroy = 559); the render/tile API provides guaranteed 256x256 or 512x512 card art (JPG/WebP/PNG) — download once, precompute hashes, ship them in-app. | [high] The deckstring format lets the user import their own deck as ground truth, which collapses the recognition problem: instead of open-set recognition over ~4000 cards, DeckView matches observed cards against 30 known candidates. This is the highest-leverage move for BOTH accuracy and stability (smaller candidate set = faster, cheaper, more reliable matching). | [high] Realistically extractable state, ranked by reliability: game PHASE/scene (menu/mulligan/in-game/victory) via cheap ROI fingerprints > hero/class (fixed portrait ROIs) > mana crystals & turn (count blue gems / read a small number) > the card being played (animates large to board center — the single best card-recognition target) > board minions (larger than hand cards) > mulligan hand (3-4 large cards, good target) >> cards fanned in hand (small, overlapping — hardest). The deck's hidden contents are NOT observable; you can only track drawn/played events, same as any tracker. | [medium] On-device OCR of card names is a viable SECONDARY/disambiguation channel: use Google ML Kit Text Recognition (on-device, free, zero-latency, privacy-friendly) rather than Tesseract — ML Kit is ~20-40% more accurate on Android and needs no network. Use it to break pHash ties (e.g. golden vs normal, similar art) and to read numbers (mana cost, turn). | [medium] The 800x360 resolution the spike harness captured at is a real constraint: full-screen at that size makes fanned in-hand card ART too small for reliable pHash. Recognition should target large elements (played-card animation, board minions, mulligan, gems) and/or capture ROIs at higher resolution. Raising resolution costs CPU/memory, which directly trades against the STABILITY-FIRST mandate — so it must be selective and off-thread. | [medium] Free Gemini 2.5-flash vision is a good on-demand fallback for hard scenes (reading a cluttered board, verifying an ambiguous mulligan) but MUST stay out of the hot per-frame loop — invoke it occasionally/on-demand with a batched screenshot, never as the streaming recognizer. This respects the free-API preference and the >=$0.10 authorization rule while keeping latency off the render path.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Architect the pipeline as a state machine driven OFF the capture/UI thread. Stage 1 (cheap, every processed frame): classify game PHASE via a few small ROI fingerprints. Stage 2 (only in relevant phases, and only on STABLE frames detected by frame-diff): run pHash card/board recognition. Never run CV inside the MediaProjection ImageReader callback or on the main thread — this directly addresses the diagnosed main-thread-freeze risk. | Make deckstring import a first-class, prominent feature. Let the user paste their deck code (base64/varint per HearthSim spec); decode to a 30-card dbfId candidate set and constrain in-game recognition to those cards + observed opponent cards. This is the biggest single win for accuracy, speed, and stability. | Use pHash (64-bit) + Hamming-distance matching over fixed ROIs as the primary recognizer; precompute the reference hash DB offline from HearthstoneJSON 256x/512x tile art and ship it in-app (no runtime downloads, works offline, no per-frame network). Key everything on dbfId so it maps cleanly to deckstrings and HearthstoneJSON metadata. | Prioritize recognizing LARGE, unambiguous elements: the card being played (large center animation), mulligan cards, and board minions — not the small fanned hand. Detect 'a card was played/drawn' as an EVENT rather than trying to continuously classify every hand card. | Add Google ML Kit on-device OCR (free, offline) as a disambiguation/number-reading channel (mana cost, turn counter, tie-breaking similar art). Do NOT use Tesseract. | Capture at a resolution high enough for card-art discrimination but recognize on selectively-cropped ROIs; benchmark on-device to find the minimum resolution that keeps pHash reliable while holding frame processing time low. Treat resolution as a stability/accuracy tradeoff dial, tuned empirically. | Reserve free Gemini 2.5-flash vision strictly for on-demand, batched 'hard scene' reads (never per-frame) — keeping it off the render path preserves the zero-freeze mandate and stays within the free-tier / >=$0.10 rules. | Reuse the existing dev.lyai.deckview.spike harness as the capture/eventing backbone, but move all capture-encode-write work to a background queue (as the perf diagnosis already recommended) so measurement and recognition never contend with the UI thread. | Study open-source prior art for concrete ROI/pHash code: HearthSim/python-hearthstone + hearthstone-deckstrings (data + deckstrings), Arena Helper and wittenbe/Hearthstone-Image-Recognition (pHash recognition), even though all are PC/high-res — port the technique, not the resolution assumptions.
RISKS: (high) Running computer vision on or near the capture/UI thread reintroduces exactly the multi-second freezes the perf diagnosis found (main-thread blocking). Per-frame CV without gating would be catastrophic for the zero-crash mandate. -> Strict off-thread pipeline + event-driven gating (scene-change/stable-frame triggers, phase state machine). Recognition runs on a background dispatcher; the render/chat thread is fully decoupled. Load-test worst case (long chat message on screen WHILE a board is being recognized). | (high) 800x360-class capture resolution is likely too low to reliably pHash small fanned hand cards, causing misidentification or low match confidence. -> Recognize from large elements (played-card animation, board, mulligan) instead of the hand; raise ROI capture resolution selectively; require a Hamming-distance confidence threshold and abstain (mark 'unknown') rather than guess. Empirically validate on-device before committing. | (medium) Card database churns constantly (new sets ~3x/year, nerfs, new golden/diamond/signature art variants). A shipped reference-hash DB goes stale, silently degrading recognition. -> Design the reference hash DB as an updatable asset regenerated from HearthstoneJSON on each patch; version it; deckstring import (ground-truth dbfIds) buys resilience since matching is constrained to known cards even if art shifts slightly. | (medium) Screen contents are potentially sensitive (MediaProjection captures the whole screen, notifications included) and continuous capture is CPU/battery heavy — a UX and privacy liability. -> Keep all recognition on-device (pHash + ML Kit) with no frame upload; gate Gemini calls to explicit on-demand use with user awareness; throttle capture aggressively (event-driven, low FPS when idle); crop to the game window ROI early and discard full frames immediately. | (medium) OCR of stylized Hearthstone fonts over busy art backgrounds is unreliable, so leaning on card-name OCR as a primary signal would produce errors. -> Use OCR only as a tie-breaker/number-reader behind pHash, not as the primary recognizer; constrain expected text to the imported deck's card names (fuzzy-match OCR output against a small known list). | (low) Anti-cheat/ToS ambiguity: an app that reads the game screen and advises the player could be viewed differently from a passive overlay. Screen-capture assistants sit in a grayer area than log-based trackers on PC. -> Flag to Ignacio for a product/ToS decision; keep the app strictly observational/informational (no input automation), which is how deck tracking has historically been tolerated.
OPEN Qs: What is the exact target device/screen resolution and the game-window aspect ratio DeckView will run against? This determines whether in-hand card ROIs are recognizable and drives the resolution/stability tradeoff. | Will Hearthstone run in the foreground with DeckView as an overlay bubble, or is split-screen/second-device intended? MediaProjection can only capture the foreground; an overlay bubble that pauses capture during chat interaction may be needed. | Is deckstring import acceptable to the product owner as a required onboarding step (huge accuracy/stability win), or must recognition work fully 'blind' from screen only? | How much opponent-side tracking is in scope? Opponent deck is not importable, so opponent card recognition is strictly the open-set (harder) problem — this materially raises recognition difficulty vs tracking only the user's own deck. | What Hearthstone game modes are targeted (Standard/Wild constructed, Arena, Battlegrounds, Duels)? Battlegrounds/Arena have very different UIs and would need separate ROI maps and recognition logic.

## mediaprojection
SUMMARY: A stability-first DeckView capture pipeline should use MediaProjection + VirtualDisplay feeding an ImageReader (not MediaCodec — you need raw frames for on-device/Gemini vision, not an encoded video). Run the whole thing in a FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_MEDIA_PROJECTION service on a dedicated HandlerThread so nothing touches the UI thread. The critical correctness rules are: (a) on Android 14+ you must call createScreenCaptureIntent() and start the foreground service BEFORE getMediaProjection(), and you must registerCallback() before createVirtualDisplay() or it throws; (b) drain ImageReader with acquireLatestImage() and close() every Image immediately (missing close() is the classic silent freeze/ANR); (c) do NOT capture at display refresh rate — throttle to ~1-4 fps for card recognition, which slashes battery/thermal load and back-pressure. MediaProjection sees the whole display except FLAG_SECURE windows and system UI overlays; Hearthstone does not set FLAG_SECURE so it is capturable, but your own tracker overlay (TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY) is EXCLUDED from the capture, which is exactly what you want (no feedback loop). The freeze diagnosis in the brief is a UI-thread/Markdown problem, NOT a capture problem — but the capture pipeline must be architected off-thread from day one so it never becomes one.
KEY FINDINGS: [high] Use MediaProjection + VirtualDisplay -> ImageReader for raw frames, NOT a MediaCodec/Surface encoder path. Card recognition (on-device CV or Gemini vision) consumes still images/bitmaps, so an H.264 encoder would only add an encode+decode round-trip and latency. ImageReader.getSurface() is the documented consumer for 'frame-by-frame access, real-time processing'; MediaCodec is for recording/streaming. | [high] BACK-PRESSURE is the top pipeline-stability risk and is solved by three rules: (1) allocate ImageReader.newInstance(w,h,format, maxImages) with a small maxImages (2-3), (2) in onImageAvailable always use acquireLatestImage() (drops stale frames, keeps only newest) rather than acquireNextImage(), (3) call image.close() IMMEDIATELY after copying pixels. If you don't close Images, the buffer queue fills, the producer (SurfaceFlinger) stalls, and you get an ANR/freeze on ImageReader.acquireLatestImage. | [high] THROTTLE capture to ~1-4 fps — do NOT process every VSYNC (~60fps). Card/board/deck state changes on the scale of seconds, not milliseconds, so a low rate is sufficient and is the single biggest battery/thermal win. Implement throttling by timestamp-gating in onImageAvailable: if (now - lastProcessed < intervalMs) { image.close(); return; }. Always still acquire+close the image to avoid back-pressure even when skipping recognition. | [high] Android 14+ (target SDK 34) HARD REQUIREMENT: the capture must live in a foreground service declaring android:foregroundServiceType="mediaProjection", with both FOREGROUND_SERVICE and FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PROJECTION permissions. Order is strict: call createScreenCaptureIntent() -> user consents -> startForeground() the service -> THEN getMediaProjection(). Getting the projection before the FGS is running throws SecurityException; missing the type throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException. | [high] registerCallback() is MANDATORY before createVirtualDisplay() or it throws IllegalStateException. The MediaProjection.Callback.onStop() must release the VirtualDisplay + Surface + stop the projection. onStop() fires when the user taps the Android 15 status-bar screen-share chip, when the screen locks, when another projection starts, or when the process is killed — DeckView must handle all of these gracefully (auto-stop + offer re-consent) to satisfy the zero-crash mandate. | [high] Android 14+ requires FRESH user consent for EACH capture session: the intent from createScreenCaptureIntent() is single-use, and each MediaProjection token allows createVirtualDisplay() only ONCE. You cannot silently resume capture after onStop() — you must re-prompt. Design DeckView so a game session = one consent + one long-lived VirtualDisplay; do not tear down/recreate the display per card. Android 14 QPR2 / 15 also default the consent dialog to a full-screen-vs-single-app CHOICE. | [medium] For the tracker UI, use a SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlay of type TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY drawn on top of Hearthstone. This overlay is EXCLUDED from your own MediaProjection capture (system UI / overlay windows are not part of the mirrored display content in single-app mode, and even in full-display mode you can filter your own package), which conveniently prevents a capture-feedback loop where the tracker reads its own UI. To let game touches pass through, the overlay must use FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE and either be non-touchable regions or keep alpha <= ~0.8 (getMaximumObscuringOpacityForTouch) due to untrusted-touch restrictions. | [medium] MediaProjection can legally see any non-FLAG_SECURE app on the same device — it does NOT need to be your own app. Hearthstone (Blizzard) does not set FLAG_SECURE on gameplay, so its board/hand/deck are capturable. If it EVER did, the captured frames would be solid black (not an error), so DeckView needs a black-frame guard: detect all-black/low-variance frames and surface a graceful 'cannot read game' state rather than feeding garbage to recognition. | [high] Keep capture AND recognition entirely off the UI thread: run the MediaProjection service work on a dedicated HandlerThread, pass that Handler to createVirtualDisplay(..., handler) and ImageReader.setOnImageAvailableListener(listener, handler) so callbacks never land on main. Feed recognition (Gemini/CV) via a bounded single-item queue (drop-oldest) so a slow vision call cannot back up the capture buffer. This is architecturally independent of the chat-Markdown freeze, but it guarantees capture is never a jank source.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Architecture: one foreground service (foregroundServiceType=mediaProjection) owns a HandlerThread; MediaProjection -> VirtualDisplay -> ImageReader(maxImages=2-3, format RGBA_8888 or RGB_565) with its OnImageAvailableListener bound to that HandlerThread's Handler. Never touch the main thread in the capture path. | Throttle to a config-driven ~2 fps (range 1-4). In onImageAvailable ALWAYS acquireLatestImage()+close(); only run recognition when the throttle interval has elapsed. This is the primary battery/thermal control and prevents buffer back-pressure. | Enforce the Android 14+ call order rigorously: createScreenCaptureIntent() -> consent result -> startForeground(mediaProjection) -> getMediaProjection() -> registerCallback() -> createVirtualDisplay(). Wrap each step with explicit failure handling (SecurityException, IllegalStateException, MissingForegroundServiceTypeException) so a denied/expired consent degrades gracefully, never crashes. | Treat every onStop() (status-bar stop chip, screen lock, another projection, process death) as a first-class state: release VirtualDisplay+Surface, mark capture inactive, and prompt for fresh consent on resume — remember consent/token are single-use on Android 14+, so you cannot silently restart. | Build the tracker UI as a TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission) with FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE and touch-passthrough (alpha <= 0.8 for any touchable translucent region) so Hearthstone stays fully playable; the overlay being excluded from capture also avoids a self-capture feedback loop. | Decouple recognition from capture with a bounded drop-oldest queue (capacity 1): a slow Gemini vision round-trip must drop frames, never stall the ImageReader. Copy pixels out of the Image, close() it, then hand the copy to the recognition worker. | Add a black-frame / low-variance guard before recognition to handle FLAG_SECURE screens, transitions, or letterboxing, and use MediaProjection.Callback.onCapturedContentResize to resize the VirtualDisplay on rotation/window changes so frames aren't letterboxed. | Prefer downscaled capture: create the VirtualDisplay at a reduced resolution (the spike prototype used 800x360) rather than native panel resolution — smaller buffers mean less memory bandwidth, less heat, faster vision inference, and fit Gemini 2.5-flash (free) input limits. No paid vision API needed, so no >$0.10 authorization gate.
RISKS: (high) Missing image.close() (or closing late) fills the ImageReader buffer queue, stalls SurfaceFlinger, and produces an ANR/freeze on acquireLatestImage — the exact multi-second freeze signature the brief is trying to avoid, but from the capture side. -> Mandate acquireLatestImage()+close() on every callback in a finally block, cap maxImages at 2-3, and add a watchdog log if a callback ever exceeds a few ms. | (high) Android 14/15 tightening: single-use consent token + mandatory FGS ordering + onStop on lock means naive 'start once, run forever' code throws SecurityException/IllegalStateException and crashes, violating the zero-crash rule. -> Encode the exact call order in a state machine, register onStop() before createVirtualDisplay(), and treat every stop as re-consent, not silent resume. Test on Android 14, 15, and 16 devices. | (medium) Battery drain / thermal throttling from capturing at display refresh rate or at native resolution during a long ladder session, degrading both DeckView and the game. -> Throttle to 1-4 fps, capture at reduced resolution, pause capture when the app/overlay detects Hearthstone is not foreground, and batch/skip recognition when frames are visually static (frame-diff gate). | (medium) Overlay touch-obscuring / untrusted-touch restrictions could block or intercept game input, or the overlay could be rejected, making Hearthstone unplayable. -> Use FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE, keep touchable translucent regions at alpha <= getMaximumObscuringOpacityForTouch (~0.8), make non-interactive regions FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE, and let users reposition/collapse the overlay. | (low) Hearthstone or Android could present FLAG_SECURE or protected surfaces (or the user picks single-app share of the wrong app), yielding black/garbage frames fed to recognition. -> Black-frame/low-variance guard before recognition; if the user chose single-app share, verify the captured package and prompt to re-share Hearthstone; surface a clear 'can't read the game' UI state instead of hallucinating cards.
OPEN Qs: Confirm which Android versions DeckView must support (min/target SDK). Android 14 (34) vs 15 (35) vs 16 materially change consent, FGS, and single-app-share behavior — the plan above assumes target 34+ but should be pinned. | Does the recognition path run fully on-device (bundled CV/ML model) or call Gemini 2.5-flash over the network? This drives the queue latency budget, the throttle rate, and offline behavior — and network vision has its own privacy implications for screen contents. | Exact pixel format / resolution needed by the chosen recognizer (RGBA_8888 vs RGB_565, native vs downscaled). Verify against Gemini image input limits and card-art legibility before fixing the VirtualDisplay dimensions. | Will DeckView run alongside Hearthstone via split-screen/overlay only, or does it rely on the Android 14+ single-app-share mode? Single-app share changes what the capture sees (system UI excluded) and requires handling onCapturedContentResize/onCapturedContentVisibilityChanged. | Should capture auto-pause when Hearthstone is backgrounded to save battery, and how is 'Hearthstone is foreground' detected without querying other apps' state (which Android restricts)? May need UsageStats permission or accept over-capturing.

## vision-onvscloud
SUMMARY: For continuously identifying Hearthstone cards from the MediaProjection capture stream, the pragmatic, stability-first architecture is ON-DEVICE by default with cloud Gemini 2.5-Flash as an event-gated fallback — never per-frame. The binding constraints against continuous cloud vision are (1) free-tier Requests-Per-Day caps that are far below per-frame call volume and are being cut repeatedly by Google, (2) 0.7–3s network round-trips that would violate the smooth/real-time mandate and fail entirely offline, and (3) sending screen contents to Google (privacy) plus radio-wake battery drain. On-device (ML Kit OCR for card names/mana/attack/health digits + a LiteRT embedding/classifier matched against a bundled card DB, or OpenCV template matching) runs in single-digit-to-low-tens of milliseconds, offline, free, and private. The decisive design pattern is a CHEAP on-device change-detector (downscaled luma-diff / perceptual hash) that runs at capture FPS and gates the expensive identification so it only fires when the board/hand actually changes. Reserve Gemini 2.5-Flash for the AI-chat reasoning and occasional whole-board disambiguation, throttled to a handful of calls per game. Critically for the established freeze bug: ALL vision work (on-device inference AND any network call) must run off the UI thread on a dedicated background executor with backpressure (drop frames, STRATEGY_KEEP_ONLY_LATEST), so vision can never block rendering.
KEY FINDINGS: [medium] Per-frame cloud vision is infeasible on the free tier by request-volume alone: even 1 call/sec = ~86,400 calls/day, but Gemini free-tier Requests-Per-Day for Flash has historically ranged from ~1,500/day down to as low as ~20–50/day after Google's Dec-2025 cuts. Change-gating to a few calls per game is mandatory regardless of price. | [high] Cost per frame is NOT the constraint — RPD, latency, and battery are. An 800x360 frame tokenizes to ~2 tiles (~258 tokens/tile) ≈ ~516 input tokens; at Gemini 2.5-Flash $0.30/1M input that is ~$0.00015/frame. Using media_resolution=LOW drops it to ~64–72 tokens. So a handful of gated calls per game is trivially under the $0.10 authorization threshold; the problem is only ever hitting the RPD cap or blocking on the network. | [high] ML Kit Text Recognition v2 is the strongest on-device primitive: fully offline, free, no cloud billing, no privacy exposure, Latin-script + digits, results in milliseconds, Android API 21+. It directly reads what matters most reliably — card NAMES and the mana/attack/health NUMBERS — which alone can drive deck tracking without a heavy classifier. | [high] LiteRT/TFLite (MobileNet-class, INT8-quantized, optional GPU delegate) gives few-millisecond on-device image classification/embedding suitable for matching card ART against a bundled card database via nearest-neighbor. OpenCV template matching is a simpler no-training alternative for the fixed, finite card set. Both are offline and free. | [high] Cloud Gemini 2.5-Flash's real value here is multimodal REASONING (the Markdown AI chat, whole-board 'what should I play' analysis), not per-frame OCR. It is a poor continuous-identifier because it is online-only (fails with no signal), adds 0.7–3s latency, and streams screen pixels to Google. | [high] The hybrid fast-path is the load-bearing design decision: a cheap on-device change-detector (downscaled grayscale frame-diff or 64-bit perceptual hash, sub-millisecond) runs every captured frame and only triggers the expensive identification (ML Kit/LiteRT, and rarely Gemini) when the scene is both CHANGED and STABLE (debounced). This cuts inference count, battery, and cloud calls by 1–2 orders of magnitude.
RECOMMENDATIONS: DEFAULT = on-device continuous pipeline, cloud = gated fallback. Architecture: [capture frame] -> [sub-ms change-detector: luma-diff or pHash] -> if changed+stable -> [ML Kit OCR for card names + mana/attack/health digits] + [LiteRT INT8 embedding or OpenCV template match against a bundled card-art DB] -> update deck state. Never call cloud in this loop. | Reserve Gemini 2.5-Flash for two things only: (a) the AI CHAT reasoning/answers, and (b) occasional whole-board disambiguation when on-device confidence is low. Throttle hard: target <30 cloud calls per match, debounced and cached, so you stay far under any free-tier RPD and under $0.10. | When you do call Gemini, send a downscaled/cropped region (not the raw 800x360) and set media_resolution=LOW to cut input tokens to ~64–72; batch multiple questions into one call; cache identical-frame results by perceptual hash to dedupe. | STABILITY MANDATE: run every stage — change-detection, on-device inference, and all network calls — on a dedicated background thread/coroutine, NOT the UI/render thread. Use CameraX/ImageAnalysis STRATEGY_KEEP_ONLY_LATEST (or manual frame-dropping) so a slow stage drops frames instead of queuing/blocking. This is the same class of fix as the Markdown-render freeze: keep the main thread free. | Treat cloud as best-effort and cancellable: bound every Gemini call with a short timeout, cancel superseded requests, and degrade gracefully to on-device-only when offline or rate-limited — the tracker must keep working with zero network. Never let a pending cloud call stall the capture/render loop. | Bundle a local card database (names + art thumbnails + mana/attack/health) shipped with the app and updated per set release. This makes on-device OCR/matching authoritative and keeps the pipeline offline; card sets are finite and change only a few times per year. | Prefer OCR-of-name as the primary identifier (most robust, cheapest, language-directly-usable) and use art-embedding/template-match as a secondary confirmer/tie-breaker. Only escalate to Gemini when both disagree or text is occluded. | Privacy: because captured frames may contain sensitive on-screen content, keep the continuous pipeline 100% on-device, and gate any cloud upload behind an explicit user-visible setting/disclosure. This also satisfies LyAi's on-device/privacy preference.
RISKS: (high) Google's free-tier Gemini RPD limits are volatile and were cut sharply in Dec 2025 (down to ~20–50/day for Flash in some reports). Any design that depends on frequent cloud calls can break overnight when quotas change. -> Do not put cloud on the critical path. On-device pipeline must be fully functional standalone; cloud is an enhancement. Gate + cache + throttle cloud calls and monitor 429s, degrading silently to on-device. | (high) Cloud round-trip latency (0.7–3s) and offline failure directly conflict with the smooth/real-time and zero-crash mandate if used per-frame or synchronously. -> Never call cloud synchronously or per-frame; async, timeout-bounded, cancellable, off the UI thread, with on-device fallback. | (medium) Building/maintaining a LiteRT classifier for the full ~thousands-of-cards set (which rotates each expansion) is heavy and can rot. Accuracy degrades on new sets until retrained. -> Favor OCR-of-name (no per-card training) as primary; use art matching via embedding+nearest-neighbor or template match against a bundled DB you can update with a data drop, not a model retrain. Escalate unknowns to Gemini sparingly. | (medium) On-device GPU delegate can fall back to CPU on unsupported ops and run SLOWER, and per-frame inference plus continuous capture drains battery/heats the device — which can itself cause jank/throttling. -> Benchmark CPU vs GPU delegate per device before enabling; rely on the change-detector to minimize inference count; cap pipeline FPS; drop frames under load. | (medium) Hearthstone card text (names/digits) can be small, stylized, animated, or partially occluded in-hand/on-board, hurting OCR reliability; art can be foil/animated, hurting template matching. -> Combine OCR + art matching with confidence scoring; use region-specific crops (mana crystal, name banner, attack/health corners); escalate low-confidence cases to Gemini for disambiguation, then cache the result. | (medium) Sending screen frames to Gemini exposes potentially sensitive on-screen content to a third party (privacy) and is a data-egress concern. -> Keep continuous pipeline on-device; crop to card regions before any upload; gate cloud upload behind explicit user consent/disclosure setting.
OPEN Qs: What is the CURRENT exact free-tier RPD/RPM/TPM for gemini-2.5-flash and gemini-2.5-flash-lite on Ignacio's specific account/tier? Docs now defer to the AI Studio dashboard — must be read live before committing to a call budget. | Does Hearthstone on this Android device reliably render card NAMES legibly at 800x360 capture resolution, or should capture resolution be raised for the identification path (with the change-detector still running on downscaled frames)? | Is a maintained machine-readable Hearthstone card database (names + art + stats, per set) available to bundle/update, e.g. via HearthstoneJSON, and what is its licensing for redistribution inside the app? | What is the acceptable end-to-end identification latency budget per board change (e.g. <200ms) to feel real-time, which determines whether GPU-delegate LiteRT is needed or ML Kit OCR alone suffices? | Which specific device(s)/SoC are the target so on-device inference and GPU-delegate behavior can be benchmarked (CPU-fallback risk)?

## markdown-chat
SUMMARY: The diagnosed 3.9s freezes are almost certainly synchronous Markdown parsing + full text-layout (measure) of a long message happening on the UI thread, plus (in Compose) hundreds of full re-renders during streaming. A jank-free design rests on four pillars: (1) parse Markdown to spans OFF the main thread and hand the TextView a PrecomputedText it only blocks on at measure time; (2) virtualize the chat with a RecyclerView + ListAdapter/DiffUtil (or LazyColumn with stable keys), so only visible messages render; (3) render a streaming message BLOCK-by-BLOCK and append-only, never re-parsing the whole message per token, and throttle token updates to ~1 UI update per frame (~16-60ms); (4) suppress incomplete Markdown delimiters during streaming to avoid flicker. For a Views stack, Markwon 4.6.x supports all of this today (PrecomputedTextSetterCompat with a background Executor). For Compose, prefer keeping heavy Markdown in an AndroidView(Markwon) or use an append-only incremental library; naive Compose Markdown that re-parses a growing string each token is the worst case and reproduces exactly the diagnosed bug. STABILITY-FIRST verdict: RecyclerView + Markwon + off-thread PrecomputedText is the lowest-risk, proven path.
KEY FINDINGS: [high] The freeze is main-thread text WORK (Markdown parse + StaticLayout measure), not I/O — parsing markdown and measuring a long StaticLayout are synchronous CPU tasks on the UI thread that scale with message length; a long bulleted AI message is exactly the pathological input. | [high] Markwon (Android Views, no WebView) can parse and build the Spanned OFF the main thread via PrecomputedTextSetterCompat, applying it with PrecomputedText so the TextView only blocks at measure(). | [high] PrecomputedTextCompat.getTextFuture + AppCompatTextView.setTextFuture moves text measurement to a background thread; RecyclerView prefetch gives it time to finish before bind/measure, cutting UI-thread text cost by ~95%. | [high] For STREAMING, re-parsing the entire growing message on every token is the dominant jank source; the fix is append-only / block-based rendering plus throttling token updates to roughly one UI update per frame. | [high] Incomplete Markdown delimiters during streaming cause visible flicker and must be suppressed until closed; a lightweight single-pass buffer beats heavy re-parsing. | [high] In Jetpack Compose, LazyColumn only composes visible items but the naive Markdown path (parse a growing String in composition, no stable keys) reproduces the freeze; it needs stable item keys, immutable/stable message models, and heavy parse kept out of composition. | [medium] A ready-made option exists: GetStream stream-chat-android-ai provides a Compose StreamingText (chunkDelayMs default 30ms throttle, auto-continuation when new text extends previous) plus markdown and typing indicators. | [medium] WebView is a viable but heavier alternative for rich Markdown (tables, math, syntax highlighting) and is a poor fit for the stability-first mandate here.
RECOMMENDATIONS: ADOPT (stability-first, lowest risk): Android Views + RecyclerView + Markwon 4.6.x. Build the Markwon instance once with textSetter(PrecomputedTextSetterCompat.create(backgroundExecutor)) so every message's spans are parsed and precomputed off the main thread. This is the proven, documented anti-freeze path and directly kills the diagnosed bug. | VIRTUALIZE the chat list with RecyclerView + ListAdapter + DiffUtil (submitList on a background diff). Never inflate all messages; only visible + prefetched holders render. Give each message a stable id (DiffUtil areItemsTheSame by id, areContentsTheSame by content+isStreaming). If Compose is mandated, use LazyColumn with key = message.id and @Immutable message models, and keep parsing OUT of composables. | CACHE parsed output per message: parse Markdown -> Spanned exactly once per finalized message and store it (LruCache keyed by message id + content hash). Re-scrolling or rebinding must reuse the cached Spanned/PrecomputedText, never re-parse. This makes scrolling past old long messages free. | STREAM append-only and BLOCK-based: split the incoming message into Markdown blocks (split on blank lines / code-fence boundaries). Finalize and cache every block except the last still-growing one; only re-parse that trailing block per update. Never re-parse the whole message on each token — this is the single most important streaming rule. | THROTTLE token->UI updates to at most one per frame: collect tokens into a buffer and emit to the UI on a ~16-50ms cadence (e.g. Kotlin Flow with sample()/conflate(), or a coalescing Handler.post). Do NOT setText per token. Combine with an isStreaming flag. | SUPPRESS incomplete delimiters while isStreaming=true using a lightweight single-pass buffer (MarkdownBuffer pattern): count pair delimiters, hide trailing unclosed markers (**, *, `, ```), process code fences before inline code and bold before italic. On stream completion, render the full unmodified text so intentional lone markers survive. | ENFORCE off-thread parsing structurally: run all CommonMark parsing inside a coroutine on Dispatchers.Default (or Markwon's Executor). The UI thread must only receive an already-parsed Spanned/PrecomputedText and only block at measure(). When building PrecomputedTextCompat.Params, set textSize/typeface/textDir/breakStrategy to EXACTLY match the target TextView first, or measure() will throw. | HANDLE images/tables deliberately: load Markdown images via Coil/Glide async with fixed placeholder dimensions (Markwon image plugin) so late image loads don't retrigger a full relayout mid-stream; render tables as a bounded, horizontally-scrollable view. Avoid unbounded-height content that forces remeasure. | AVOID (for this mandate): naive Compose Markdown libraries that re-parse a growing String inside composition with no stable block identity, and WebView-based rendering. Both reintroduce main-thread/re-render blowups the diagnosis already caught. If a Compose look is required, wrap Markwon in AndroidView or use an append-only incremental Compose-markdown library. | INSTRUMENT anti-ANR guardrails from day one: add a StrictMode thread policy in debug to flag main-thread parsing/I-O; add a FrameMetrics/JankStats monitor asserting no frame > ~200ms while a long message renders; reuse the existing spike harness (inter_ms) as a regression gate — any inter_ms > ~700ms during a scripted long-Markdown stream is a build failure.
RISKS: (high) Choosing Jetpack Compose with a naive Markdown renderer re-parses the whole growing message every token and re-renders in composition — directly reproducing the diagnosed 3.9s freeze at the worst possible moment (streaming a long answer). -> For Compose, do heavy parse in a background flow into cached immutable blocks; render blocks in LazyColumn with stable keys; or wrap Markwon in AndroidView. Default to the Views+Markwon+PrecomputedText stack unless Compose is a hard requirement. | (medium) PrecomputedText misuse: Params (textSize/typeface/width/breakStrategy) not matching the actual TextView causes an exception at measure() or silently falls back to on-thread measurement, quietly restoring the jank. -> Set all TextView layout properties before creating Params; centralize a single text-appearance style shared by the precompute step and the view; unit-test that setTextFuture params equal the bound TextView params. | (high) Streaming token flood: emitting a UI update per token (hundreds/response) saturates the main thread with tiny setText+measure passes even if each is cheap, producing sustained micro-jank and battery drain. -> Coalesce tokens and update at most once per frame (Flow.sample(~33ms)/conflate); only re-parse the trailing block; append-only StaticLayout where possible. | (medium) Images/tables/large code blocks in a Markdown message cause a late asynchronous relayout that reflows the whole message and can jank mid-scroll or mid-stream. -> Async image loading with fixed placeholder size; bounded scrollable tables/code; avoid intrinsic-height content; measure with representative long messages containing images+tables. | (low) Adopting a heavyweight full chat SDK (e.g. GetStream) for its StreamingText brings dependency bloat, its own markdown formatter, and undocumented off-thread guarantees — harder to certify against the zero-freeze rule. -> Prototype and profile it against the spike harness before committing; prefer the minimal Markwon path if the SDK cannot demonstrate off-thread parsing and per-frame throttling under a scripted long-message stream.
OPEN Qs: Is the UI stack for DeckView's chat decided as Android Views (XML/RecyclerView) or Jetpack Compose? The recommended anti-jank implementation differs substantially and the diagnosis logs cannot tell us which was in use. | How is the AI response delivered — true token streaming (SSE/websocket, needs throttling+block rendering) or single-shot full Markdown (only needs off-thread parse + virtualization)? Gemini 2.5-flash streaming vs non-streaming changes the design. | What Markdown feature surface must be supported (tables, LaTeX/math, syntax-highlighted code, images)? Rich features push toward WebView/heavier libs and change the risk profile; a constrained subset keeps Markwon lightweight. | Does the current spike prototype already inflate the chat, or is the chat a separate not-yet-built module? Confirms whether the freeze source can be reproduced/regression-tested with existing capture harness. | Expected max message length and history depth (messages retained in the list)? Drives whether pagination/DB-backed windowing of the RecyclerView is needed on top of virtualization.

## ai-chat-integration
SUMMARY: Design for the AI "brain" of the DeckView Hearthstone assistant: a grounded, streaming, Markdown chat backed by Gemini 2.5-flash (free tier) behind a swappable LLM abstraction. The controlling constraint is the established performance diagnosis — long Markdown answers froze the UI for up to 3.9s by blocking the main thread. Therefore the chat design is stability-first: (a) ALL network + SSE parsing + Markdown parsing happens off the UI thread on a background dispatcher; (b) responses stream token-by-token into a VIRTUALIZED chat list so no single giant view is ever inflated; (c) grounding is done deterministically — the recognized deck/board/hand is resolved against a bundled HearthstoneJSON card DB and injected as structured, verified context so the model describes the CURRENT game and cannot invent cards; (d) a clean LlmClient interface isolates Gemini so Claude or an on-device model can be swapped later; (e) graceful offline/degraded behavior (deterministic tracker keeps working; chat shows a clear "assistant offline" state and queues). Two important verified caveats: Gemini free-tier limits are tight (~10 RPM / ~250-500 req/day for 2.5-flash as of 2026, cut 50-80% in Dec 2025), and free-tier prompts/responses are used by Google for product improvement WITH HUMAN REVIEW — a real privacy problem because DeckView's context is derived from screen capture.
KEY FINDINGS: [high] The #1 chat-side stability risk is rendering the Markdown answer on the UI thread; the fix is to keep BOTH markdown parsing AND stream handling off the main thread and stream into a virtualized list. Concretely: OkHttp/Retrofit call on Dispatchers.IO -> parse each SSE chunk off-thread -> emit deltas via a cold Flow -> UI collects on Main and appends plain text to the streaming bubble; run the Markdown parse (Markwon/CommonMark) on a background dispatcher and post only the finished Spanned back to the view. Never inflate one bubble containing the whole answer; the streaming bubble grows incrementally and the completed message becomes one RecyclerView item. | [high] Grounding must be deterministic, not model-guessed. Pipeline: vision recognition returns card IDs/dbfIds + board state -> resolve each ID against a BUNDLED HearthstoneJSON cards.collectible.json (offline, versioned per patch) to get canonical name/cost/text/mechanics -> build a compact structured 'GAME STATE' block (your deck list + drawn/remaining, known opponent cards, mana, board minions, turn) -> inject as a system/context section each turn. The model is told to answer ONLY from that block. This keeps answers about the CURRENT game and prevents hallucinated cards because the card facts come from the DB, not the model. | [high] Gemini streaming is available over plain REST/SSE and is well-suited to Android with no SDK: POST to v1beta/models/gemini-2.5-flash:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse with header x-goog-api-key. Each SSE line is a GenerateContentResponse whose text is at candidates[0].content.parts[0].text; concatenating the deltas yields the full answer, and Markdown is the model's natural output format. | [medium] Gemini free-tier limits are tight and volatile — plan for throttling, not abundance. For 2.5-flash in 2026, sources report ~10 RPM, ~250,000 TPM, and ~250-500 requests/day, after Google cut free-tier quotas 50-80% on 7 Dec 2025. The assistant must therefore be REQUEST-FRUGAL: do NOT call the model on every recognized frame. Trigger a model call only on (a) explicit user chat message, or (b) a meaningful discrete game event (turn start, key card played), debounced/coalesced, with a client-side rate limiter and 429 backoff. The deterministic tracker (deck/board display) must never depend on a model call. | [high] PRIVACY RISK requiring Ignacio's decision: on the Gemini FREE tier, prompts and responses are used to improve Google products and may undergo HUMAN REVIEW; only the PAID tier guarantees data is not used for training. DeckView's context is derived from live SCREEN CAPTURE, so recognized game state (and anything the vision layer captures) would be sent to Google under free-tier terms. Mitigations: send ONLY the minimal structured game-state block and the user's typed question (never raw screenshots to the chat model), strip any incidental PII, and flag to Ignacio that true privacy requires the paid tier (a >=$0.10 cost decision) or an on-device model. | [high] A thin LlmClient abstraction makes the model swappable (Gemini -> Claude -> on-device) without touching UI or grounding code. Define: interface LlmClient { fun streamChat(system: String, gameState: GameStateContext, history: List<Turn>, userMsg: String): Flow<Delta> }. GeminiClient maps this to streamGenerateContent+SSE; a future ClaudeClient maps to the Messages streaming API; a Null/OfflineClient returns a canned degraded response. Prompt assembly and Markdown rendering are provider-agnostic and live above the interface. | [medium] Context-window / conversation state should be a rolling, bounded structure: keep a short conversation history (last N user/assistant turns) PLUS a freshly-recomputed GAME STATE block each turn (the game state supersedes stale history, so old board states are dropped rather than accumulated). This keeps token usage low (protecting the TPM/RPD budget) and keeps the model anchored to the live game instead of a long transcript. Persist the session (Room/DataStore) so a process restart or the documented session-limit cutoff does not lose the chat.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Architect the chat as a unidirectional pipeline off the UI thread: OkHttp SSE call on Dispatchers.IO -> per-chunk parse -> Flow<Delta> -> UI appends plain text to a single streaming bubble; parse Markdown (Markwon) on a background dispatcher and post only the finished Spanned. This is the direct countermeasure to the 3.9s freeze diagnosis. | Render the chat in a RecyclerView (virtualized) with paging; the in-progress answer is ONE streaming item, completed answers are individual items. Never build a monolithic view holding an entire long answer. | Bundle a versioned HearthstoneJSON cards.collectible.json in-app for OFFLINE, deterministic card resolution; resolve recognized card IDs/dbfIds to canonical facts BEFORE prompting so the model never has to remember card data (kills the main hallucination vector). | Inject a compact structured GAME STATE block each turn and instruct the model to answer only from it; recompute it fresh rather than accumulating stale board history to save tokens. | Use REST streaming: gemini-2.5-flash:streamGenerateContent?alt=sse with x-goog-api-key; read candidates[0].content.parts[0].text deltas. Avoid pulling the full SDK if a lean OkHttp client suffices for stability/size. | Be request-frugal: call the model ONLY on explicit user messages or debounced discrete game events, with a client-side rate limiter and exponential backoff on HTTP 429. Keep the deterministic deck/board tracker fully independent of any model call. | Put a swappable LlmClient interface (Flow<Delta> streaming) between the app and Gemini so Claude or an on-device model can be dropped in later without touching UI/grounding. | Design explicit degraded states: OfflineClient / no-network -> show 'Assistant offline, deck tracking still active' and queue the user question; on repeated 429 -> show 'rate-limited, retrying' with backoff; never crash or block on a failed model call. | Escalate the privacy decision to Ignacio: free-tier Gemini uses prompts+responses for training with human review. Send only minimal structured game state + typed questions (never raw screenshots to the chat model); note that true privacy needs the paid tier (a >=$0.10 authorization) or an on-device model. | Persist the chat session (Room/DataStore) so the assistant survives process death and the documented session-limit cutoffs; reload bounded history on restart.
RISKS: (high) Repeating the original defect: parsing a long Markdown answer or inflating a large chat view on the UI thread reintroduces multi-second freezes and violates the zero-crash/PDS Gold mandate. -> Mandate off-UI-thread SSE + Markdown parsing, incremental streaming into a virtualized RecyclerView, and a max-render-chunk cap; add a StrictMode/thread-time assertion in debug and a synthetic 'very long answer' test in the harness. | (high) Gemini free-tier quotas are tight (~10 RPM / ~250-500 RPD for 2.5-flash) and were cut 50-80% in Dec 2025; per-frame or chatty usage will hit 429s and make the assistant feel broken. -> Event-debounced, rate-limited requests with 429 backoff; deterministic tracker independent of the model; cache/reuse answers; surface a clear rate-limited UI state instead of hanging. | (high) Free-tier data policy: screen-capture-derived game state and user questions are sent to Google and may be used for training with human review — a privacy exposure for potentially sensitive screen content. -> Send only minimal structured state (no raw screenshots to the chat model); PII-strip; escalate paid-tier (>=$0.10) or on-device model choice to Ignacio as an explicit decision. | (medium) Hallucinated cards / wrong game facts erode trust in a competitive tool if the model is asked to recall card data or infer board state. -> Deterministic HearthstoneJSON resolution of all card facts before prompting; instruct model to answer only from the injected verified state and to say 'unknown' rather than guess; validate any card names the model emits against the DB before display. | (medium) Model/API drift: by 2026 Google shipped Gemini 3 / a newer Interactions API and deprecates preview model IDs; a hardcoded gemini-2.5-flash-preview endpoint may break. -> Isolate the endpoint/model ID behind the LlmClient and remote-config the model name; monitor for deprecation; the abstraction lets you move to a current model or Claude with one implementation change. | (low) Unbounded conversation history inflates token usage (blowing the TPM budget) and dilutes grounding with stale board states. -> Bounded rolling history (last N turns) + fresh game-state block each turn that supersedes old state; measure token usage against the live TPM limit and tune N.
OPEN Qs: Exact current free-tier limits for gemini-2.5-flash are project-specific and vary across 2026 sources (~10 RPM, ~250K TPM, ~250-500 RPD) — confirm the real numbers in the target project's Google AI Studio rate-limit view before finalizing the rate limiter. | Will Ignacio accept free-tier data-usage terms (training + human review of screen-derived context), or is paid tier / on-device required? This is a cost+privacy decision (>=$0.10 threshold). | Should DeckView adopt the newer Gemini 'Interactions API' (stateful) or stay on the classic streamGenerateContent endpoint for maximum control and a leaner Android footprint? | What is the target answer length/verbosity? A max-output-tokens cap directly bounds render cost and TPM usage and should be set deliberately given the freeze history. | Is vision (card recognition) using the SAME Gemini call as chat, or a separate pipeline? This affects request budgeting and whether screenshots ever reach the chat model.

=== YOUR ARCHITECTURE ANGLE: hybrid-balanced ===
PRIORITY = pragmatic balance. On-device CHEAP fast-path detects WHEN something changed (a card entered hand/board) and crops the region; CLOUD Gemini identifies the card only for changed regions (bounded cost). Aggressive stability guards everywhere. Deckstring import as fallback. This should be the hard-to-beat middle option.

Design a complete END-TO-END architecture for DeckView from scratch under this angle. Be concrete: name the tech stack (Kotlin? Compose vs Views? DI? persistence?), the module breakdown under dev.lyai.deckview.*, the full data flow (capture -> recognition -> state store -> tracker UI + AI chat), the recognition approach, and EXACTLY how it prevents the diagnosed main-thread markdown freeze and guarantees crash-safety. Respect the free-API/cost constraints.

### **You** `01:00`

PROJECT: DeckView — an Android app to be BUILT FROM SCRATCH (no existing source code exists). Product owner: Ignacio (LyAi Labs). Package namespace: dev.lyai.deckview.*

PRODUCT: A Hearthstone deck tracker with an integrated AI CHAT interface (assistant answers in Markdown).

CONFIRMED CORE INPUT MECHANISM (decided by product owner): real-time SCREEN CAPTURE via Android MediaProjection. Hearthstone runs on the SAME Android device; DeckView observes the game screen, recognizes cards / board / deck state via computer vision or AI, tracks the deck, and an AI chat comments and answers questions in Markdown.
WHY screen-capture (not log parsing): on Android you CANNOT read another app's files (sandbox), unlike PC trackers (Hearthstone Deck Tracker, Firestone) that parse Power.log. Screen capture + vision is the only viable on-device path.

ALREADY BUILT (prototype to reuse/learn from): dev.lyai.deckview.spike — a MediaProjection screen-capture harness. Captures 800x360 at ~33-60fps, logs per-frame proc_ms/inter_ms and process CPU, and dumps JPEG frames on jank (2 FPS "dataset" mode). It is effectively the prototype of the capture pipeline.

PERFORMANCE DIAGNOSIS (established with high confidence from real capture logs — bake these lessons into the plan):
- Per-frame processing is trivial (proc_ms ~2ms median). Not compute-bound.
- The app suffered multi-second UI FREEZES: inter-frame gaps up to 3.9s, costing 26-55% of wall-clock time in sessions where a LONG Markdown AI chat message was on screen.
- Capture-process CPU DROPS during freezes and an independent ~2s timer NEVER stalled -> the freeze is a BLOCKED render/UI thread waiting on something, NOT heavy compute and NOT OS suspension.
- Freezes correlated with rendering LONG Markdown chat messages, NOT with the capture/JPEG-dump machinery (the session that dumped the most frames was the SMOOTHEST).
- CONCLUSION: the #1 stability risk is MAIN-THREAD BLOCKING while rendering long Markdown chat messages. The architecture MUST parse/measure Markdown OFF the UI thread, virtualize the chat list, and stream/paginate incrementally.

HARD PRIORITY (product owner): STABILITY FIRST — zero crashes, smooth end-to-end (LyAi "PDS Gold Rule": no crashes in production, 99.99% uptime). Accuracy and features are secondary to never freezing/crashing.

LyAi ORGANIZATION CONSTRAINTS (must respect in every recommendation):
- Any action costing >= $0.10 requires explicit authorization from Ignacio.
- STRONGLY prefer FREE APIs: Gemini 2.5-flash (free) is the default for vision + chat. Avoid paid APIs (Imagen 4, Google Places, paid cloud vision) unless flagged as needing authorization.
- Privacy/on-device is a plus; screen contents may be sensitive.
- This exercise is PLANNING ONLY. No build/deploy. "Propuesta antes de aplicar."


=== RESEARCH DIGEST (all dimensions) ===
## hs-recognition
SUMMARY: On Android, screen capture + computer vision is the only viable path to read Hearthstone game state, because the OS sandbox blocks reading another app's Power.log (what every PC tracker — HDT, Firestone, HSTracker — actually uses). From rendered frames you can realistically extract game PHASE, hero/class, mana crystals, turn, mulligan hand, the card currently being played (it animates large to center — easiest target), board minions, and hero power/secrets. The proven recognition technique for Hearthstone specifically is perceptual hashing (pHash + Hamming distance) of fixed screen ROIs against a precomputed reference DB, NOT OpenCV template matching (documented as inaccurate/slow for a growing card set). The authoritative card DB is HearthstoneJSON (cardId + numeric dbfId, plus a 256x/512x card-art render API to build the reference hashes); decks and card counts are encoded as the base64/varint deckstring keyed on dbfId, with reference tooling in HearthSim's python-hearthstone / hearthstone-deckstrings. The single biggest accuracy AND stability lever is to have the user IMPORT their own deck as a deckstring: recognition then only has to match drawn/played cards against 30 known candidates rather than the full ~4000-card open set. Critically for the STABILITY-FIRST mandate: recognition must run entirely OFF the capture/UI thread, be event-driven (triggered on scene-change/stable frames, not every frame), and the 800x360 resolution the spike harness used is too low for reliable in-hand card-ART recognition — you must recognize from large elements (played-card animation, board minions, gems, OCR'd names) and/or raise ROI resolution selectively.
KEY FINDINGS: [high] Screen capture is genuinely the only on-device option: Android's app sandbox prevents DeckView from reading Hearthstone's Power.log, which is exactly what every mainstream PC tracker relies on (log parsing + memory reading). No mainstream on-device Android screen-recognition tracker exists — this validates the approach's novelty but also means little prior art to copy. | [high] Perceptual hashing (pHash, 64-bit, Hamming-distance match) of fixed screen ROIs is the field-proven technique for Hearthstone card/hero recognition and should be the primary method — not OpenCV template matching, which is documented as inaccurate and slow for a growing card database due to scale/lighting/distortion variation. | [high] HearthstoneJSON is the authoritative card DB and also serves the reference art needed to build the pHash database. Cards have a string cardId (e.g. EX1_001) and a numeric dbfId (e.g. Leeroy = 559); the render/tile API provides guaranteed 256x256 or 512x512 card art (JPG/WebP/PNG) — download once, precompute hashes, ship them in-app. | [high] The deckstring format lets the user import their own deck as ground truth, which collapses the recognition problem: instead of open-set recognition over ~4000 cards, DeckView matches observed cards against 30 known candidates. This is the highest-leverage move for BOTH accuracy and stability (smaller candidate set = faster, cheaper, more reliable matching). | [high] Realistically extractable state, ranked by reliability: game PHASE/scene (menu/mulligan/in-game/victory) via cheap ROI fingerprints > hero/class (fixed portrait ROIs) > mana crystals & turn (count blue gems / read a small number) > the card being played (animates large to board center — the single best card-recognition target) > board minions (larger than hand cards) > mulligan hand (3-4 large cards, good target) >> cards fanned in hand (small, overlapping — hardest). The deck's hidden contents are NOT observable; you can only track drawn/played events, same as any tracker. | [medium] On-device OCR of card names is a viable SECONDARY/disambiguation channel: use Google ML Kit Text Recognition (on-device, free, zero-latency, privacy-friendly) rather than Tesseract — ML Kit is ~20-40% more accurate on Android and needs no network. Use it to break pHash ties (e.g. golden vs normal, similar art) and to read numbers (mana cost, turn). | [medium] The 800x360 resolution the spike harness captured at is a real constraint: full-screen at that size makes fanned in-hand card ART too small for reliable pHash. Recognition should target large elements (played-card animation, board minions, mulligan, gems) and/or capture ROIs at higher resolution. Raising resolution costs CPU/memory, which directly trades against the STABILITY-FIRST mandate — so it must be selective and off-thread. | [medium] Free Gemini 2.5-flash vision is a good on-demand fallback for hard scenes (reading a cluttered board, verifying an ambiguous mulligan) but MUST stay out of the hot per-frame loop — invoke it occasionally/on-demand with a batched screenshot, never as the streaming recognizer. This respects the free-API preference and the >=$0.10 authorization rule while keeping latency off the render path.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Architect the pipeline as a state machine driven OFF the capture/UI thread. Stage 1 (cheap, every processed frame): classify game PHASE via a few small ROI fingerprints. Stage 2 (only in relevant phases, and only on STABLE frames detected by frame-diff): run pHash card/board recognition. Never run CV inside the MediaProjection ImageReader callback or on the main thread — this directly addresses the diagnosed main-thread-freeze risk. | Make deckstring import a first-class, prominent feature. Let the user paste their deck code (base64/varint per HearthSim spec); decode to a 30-card dbfId candidate set and constrain in-game recognition to those cards + observed opponent cards. This is the biggest single win for accuracy, speed, and stability. | Use pHash (64-bit) + Hamming-distance matching over fixed ROIs as the primary recognizer; precompute the reference hash DB offline from HearthstoneJSON 256x/512x tile art and ship it in-app (no runtime downloads, works offline, no per-frame network). Key everything on dbfId so it maps cleanly to deckstrings and HearthstoneJSON metadata. | Prioritize recognizing LARGE, unambiguous elements: the card being played (large center animation), mulligan cards, and board minions — not the small fanned hand. Detect 'a card was played/drawn' as an EVENT rather than trying to continuously classify every hand card. | Add Google ML Kit on-device OCR (free, offline) as a disambiguation/number-reading channel (mana cost, turn counter, tie-breaking similar art). Do NOT use Tesseract. | Capture at a resolution high enough for card-art discrimination but recognize on selectively-cropped ROIs; benchmark on-device to find the minimum resolution that keeps pHash reliable while holding frame processing time low. Treat resolution as a stability/accuracy tradeoff dial, tuned empirically. | Reserve free Gemini 2.5-flash vision strictly for on-demand, batched 'hard scene' reads (never per-frame) — keeping it off the render path preserves the zero-freeze mandate and stays within the free-tier / >=$0.10 rules. | Reuse the existing dev.lyai.deckview.spike harness as the capture/eventing backbone, but move all capture-encode-write work to a background queue (as the perf diagnosis already recommended) so measurement and recognition never contend with the UI thread. | Study open-source prior art for concrete ROI/pHash code: HearthSim/python-hearthstone + hearthstone-deckstrings (data + deckstrings), Arena Helper and wittenbe/Hearthstone-Image-Recognition (pHash recognition), even though all are PC/high-res — port the technique, not the resolution assumptions.
RISKS: (high) Running computer vision on or near the capture/UI thread reintroduces exactly the multi-second freezes the perf diagnosis found (main-thread blocking). Per-frame CV without gating would be catastrophic for the zero-crash mandate. -> Strict off-thread pipeline + event-driven gating (scene-change/stable-frame triggers, phase state machine). Recognition runs on a background dispatcher; the render/chat thread is fully decoupled. Load-test worst case (long chat message on screen WHILE a board is being recognized). | (high) 800x360-class capture resolution is likely too low to reliably pHash small fanned hand cards, causing misidentification or low match confidence. -> Recognize from large elements (played-card animation, board, mulligan) instead of the hand; raise ROI capture resolution selectively; require a Hamming-distance confidence threshold and abstain (mark 'unknown') rather than guess. Empirically validate on-device before committing. | (medium) Card database churns constantly (new sets ~3x/year, nerfs, new golden/diamond/signature art variants). A shipped reference-hash DB goes stale, silently degrading recognition. -> Design the reference hash DB as an updatable asset regenerated from HearthstoneJSON on each patch; version it; deckstring import (ground-truth dbfIds) buys resilience since matching is constrained to known cards even if art shifts slightly. | (medium) Screen contents are potentially sensitive (MediaProjection captures the whole screen, notifications included) and continuous capture is CPU/battery heavy — a UX and privacy liability. -> Keep all recognition on-device (pHash + ML Kit) with no frame upload; gate Gemini calls to explicit on-demand use with user awareness; throttle capture aggressively (event-driven, low FPS when idle); crop to the game window ROI early and discard full frames immediately. | (medium) OCR of stylized Hearthstone fonts over busy art backgrounds is unreliable, so leaning on card-name OCR as a primary signal would produce errors. -> Use OCR only as a tie-breaker/number-reader behind pHash, not as the primary recognizer; constrain expected text to the imported deck's card names (fuzzy-match OCR output against a small known list). | (low) Anti-cheat/ToS ambiguity: an app that reads the game screen and advises the player could be viewed differently from a passive overlay. Screen-capture assistants sit in a grayer area than log-based trackers on PC. -> Flag to Ignacio for a product/ToS decision; keep the app strictly observational/informational (no input automation), which is how deck tracking has historically been tolerated.
OPEN Qs: What is the exact target device/screen resolution and the game-window aspect ratio DeckView will run against? This determines whether in-hand card ROIs are recognizable and drives the resolution/stability tradeoff. | Will Hearthstone run in the foreground with DeckView as an overlay bubble, or is split-screen/second-device intended? MediaProjection can only capture the foreground; an overlay bubble that pauses capture during chat interaction may be needed. | Is deckstring import acceptable to the product owner as a required onboarding step (huge accuracy/stability win), or must recognition work fully 'blind' from screen only? | How much opponent-side tracking is in scope? Opponent deck is not importable, so opponent card recognition is strictly the open-set (harder) problem — this materially raises recognition difficulty vs tracking only the user's own deck. | What Hearthstone game modes are targeted (Standard/Wild constructed, Arena, Battlegrounds, Duels)? Battlegrounds/Arena have very different UIs and would need separate ROI maps and recognition logic.

## mediaprojection
SUMMARY: A stability-first DeckView capture pipeline should use MediaProjection + VirtualDisplay feeding an ImageReader (not MediaCodec — you need raw frames for on-device/Gemini vision, not an encoded video). Run the whole thing in a FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_MEDIA_PROJECTION service on a dedicated HandlerThread so nothing touches the UI thread. The critical correctness rules are: (a) on Android 14+ you must call createScreenCaptureIntent() and start the foreground service BEFORE getMediaProjection(), and you must registerCallback() before createVirtualDisplay() or it throws; (b) drain ImageReader with acquireLatestImage() and close() every Image immediately (missing close() is the classic silent freeze/ANR); (c) do NOT capture at display refresh rate — throttle to ~1-4 fps for card recognition, which slashes battery/thermal load and back-pressure. MediaProjection sees the whole display except FLAG_SECURE windows and system UI overlays; Hearthstone does not set FLAG_SECURE so it is capturable, but your own tracker overlay (TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY) is EXCLUDED from the capture, which is exactly what you want (no feedback loop). The freeze diagnosis in the brief is a UI-thread/Markdown problem, NOT a capture problem — but the capture pipeline must be architected off-thread from day one so it never becomes one.
KEY FINDINGS: [high] Use MediaProjection + VirtualDisplay -> ImageReader for raw frames, NOT a MediaCodec/Surface encoder path. Card recognition (on-device CV or Gemini vision) consumes still images/bitmaps, so an H.264 encoder would only add an encode+decode round-trip and latency. ImageReader.getSurface() is the documented consumer for 'frame-by-frame access, real-time processing'; MediaCodec is for recording/streaming. | [high] BACK-PRESSURE is the top pipeline-stability risk and is solved by three rules: (1) allocate ImageReader.newInstance(w,h,format, maxImages) with a small maxImages (2-3), (2) in onImageAvailable always use acquireLatestImage() (drops stale frames, keeps only newest) rather than acquireNextImage(), (3) call image.close() IMMEDIATELY after copying pixels. If you don't close Images, the buffer queue fills, the producer (SurfaceFlinger) stalls, and you get an ANR/freeze on ImageReader.acquireLatestImage. | [high] THROTTLE capture to ~1-4 fps — do NOT process every VSYNC (~60fps). Card/board/deck state changes on the scale of seconds, not milliseconds, so a low rate is sufficient and is the single biggest battery/thermal win. Implement throttling by timestamp-gating in onImageAvailable: if (now - lastProcessed < intervalMs) { image.close(); return; }. Always still acquire+close the image to avoid back-pressure even when skipping recognition. | [high] Android 14+ (target SDK 34) HARD REQUIREMENT: the capture must live in a foreground service declaring android:foregroundServiceType="mediaProjection", with both FOREGROUND_SERVICE and FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PROJECTION permissions. Order is strict: call createScreenCaptureIntent() -> user consents -> startForeground() the service -> THEN getMediaProjection(). Getting the projection before the FGS is running throws SecurityException; missing the type throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException. | [high] registerCallback() is MANDATORY before createVirtualDisplay() or it throws IllegalStateException. The MediaProjection.Callback.onStop() must release the VirtualDisplay + Surface + stop the projection. onStop() fires when the user taps the Android 15 status-bar screen-share chip, when the screen locks, when another projection starts, or when the process is killed — DeckView must handle all of these gracefully (auto-stop + offer re-consent) to satisfy the zero-crash mandate. | [high] Android 14+ requires FRESH user consent for EACH capture session: the intent from createScreenCaptureIntent() is single-use, and each MediaProjection token allows createVirtualDisplay() only ONCE. You cannot silently resume capture after onStop() — you must re-prompt. Design DeckView so a game session = one consent + one long-lived VirtualDisplay; do not tear down/recreate the display per card. Android 14 QPR2 / 15 also default the consent dialog to a full-screen-vs-single-app CHOICE. | [medium] For the tracker UI, use a SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW overlay of type TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY drawn on top of Hearthstone. This overlay is EXCLUDED from your own MediaProjection capture (system UI / overlay windows are not part of the mirrored display content in single-app mode, and even in full-display mode you can filter your own package), which conveniently prevents a capture-feedback loop where the tracker reads its own UI. To let game touches pass through, the overlay must use FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE and either be non-touchable regions or keep alpha <= ~0.8 (getMaximumObscuringOpacityForTouch) due to untrusted-touch restrictions. | [medium] MediaProjection can legally see any non-FLAG_SECURE app on the same device — it does NOT need to be your own app. Hearthstone (Blizzard) does not set FLAG_SECURE on gameplay, so its board/hand/deck are capturable. If it EVER did, the captured frames would be solid black (not an error), so DeckView needs a black-frame guard: detect all-black/low-variance frames and surface a graceful 'cannot read game' state rather than feeding garbage to recognition. | [high] Keep capture AND recognition entirely off the UI thread: run the MediaProjection service work on a dedicated HandlerThread, pass that Handler to createVirtualDisplay(..., handler) and ImageReader.setOnImageAvailableListener(listener, handler) so callbacks never land on main. Feed recognition (Gemini/CV) via a bounded single-item queue (drop-oldest) so a slow vision call cannot back up the capture buffer. This is architecturally independent of the chat-Markdown freeze, but it guarantees capture is never a jank source.
RECOMMENDATIONS: Architecture: one foreground service (foregroundServiceType=mediaProjection) owns a HandlerThread; MediaProjection -> VirtualDisplay -> ImageReader(maxImages=2-3, format RGBA_8888 or RGB_565) with its OnImageAvailableListener bound to that HandlerThread's Handler. Never touch the main thread in the capture path. | Throttle to a config-driven ~2 fps (range 1-4). In onImageAvailable ALWAYS acquireLatestImage()+close(); only run recognition when the throttle interval has elapsed. This is the primary battery/thermal control and prevents buffer back-pressure. | Enforce the Android 14+ call order rigorously: createScreenCaptureIntent() -> consent result -> startForeground(mediaProjection) -> getMediaProjection() -> registerCallback() -> createVirtualDisplay(). Wrap each step with explicit failure handling (SecurityException, IllegalStateException, MissingForegroundServiceTypeException) so a denied/expired consent degrades gracefully, never crashes. | Treat every onStop() (status-bar stop chip, screen lock, another projection, process death) as a first-class state: release VirtualDisplay+Surface, mark capture inactive, and prompt for fresh consent on resume — remember consent/token are single-use on Android 14+, so you cannot silently restart. | Build the tracker UI as a TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY (SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission) with FLAG_NOT_FOCUSABLE and touch-passthrough (alpha <= 0.8 for any touchable translucent region) so Hearthstone stays fully playable; the overlay being excluded from capture also avoids a self-capture feedback loop. | Decouple recognition from capture with a bounded drop-oldest queue (capacity 1): a slow Gemini vision round-trip must drop frames, never stall the ImageReader.
